findings.title: Multiple equal-order crypto providers are now silently resolved by classpath order
findings.body:
`detectProvider` used to throw when more than one `CryptoProvider` was found. It now sorts by `order()` and takes the first. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return 200, so a tie between them is broken only by the stable sort, i.e. by `ServiceLoader`/classpath order. The ignored providers are logged at DEBUG only.

Consequence: a deployment that relies on `CryptoIntegration.init` (not `setProvider`) and has both the FIPS and the default crypto jars on the classpath now silently picks one at random instead of failing. It may run in non-FIPS mode without any visible warning.

All discovered providers are also instantiated before sorting. The constructors of `FIPS1402Provider` and `DefaultCryptoProvider` change JVM-global state: they insert BCFIPS/BCJSSE/KeycloakFipsSecurityProvider at positions 1-3, add BC, and rewrite `ssl.KeyManagerFactory.algorithm`. A provider that loses the tie still leaves those changes behind. Before this PR startup aborted in that case.

Suggested fix: keep the hard failure (or at least WARN) when the two highest-ranked providers have the same `order()`, and only drop lower-ranked ones.

findings.title: New abstract `order()` breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body:
`int order()` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` SPI as an abstract method. Any external or custom implementation no longer compiles.

Binaries compiled against the previous `keycloak-common` are worse: when such a provider is discovered, `Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order)` in `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` throws `AbstractMethodError` during the sort. That aborts crypto initialization entirely, even if a valid built-in provider is also present.

A `default int order() { return 0; }` (or similar) would keep the SPI backward compatible while still letting the built-in providers take precedence.

findings.title: ES384/ES512 tests use a P-256 key, so long-form DER lengths are never tested and only a self-roundtrip is checked
findings.body:
The test builds one key pair with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, which defaults to P-256, and reuses it for ES256, ES384 and ES512. With a P-256 key, r and s are at most 33 bytes and the DER SEQUENCE is under 128 bytes. So the long-form length paths in the new `ASN1Encoder.writeLength` and `ASN1Decoder.readLength` (needed for P-521/ES512, where the sequence is about 136-139 bytes) are never executed. The 48- and 66-byte component sizes are only checked as zero padding of 32-byte values.

The test also compares only the output of the hand-written decoder against itself after a round trip through the hand-written encoder. A symmetric encoding bug would pass. It never checks the re-encoded DER with `Signature.verify`, and never compares against a reference implementation such as BC.

Suggested fix: generate a key on the matching curve (secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) for each algorithm, and assert that `signature.verify(asn1Des)` succeeds.
